**TrueLayer acquires Dutch BNPL firm to add credit at checkout**

*The acquisition of In3 signals that open banking payment networks now see embedded credit as essential to competing with cards at the point of sale.*

TrueLayer has acquired In3, a Dutch consumer credit fintech that offers buy now, pay later via bank payments. The company confirmed that BNPL will be its first credit product, with longer-term lending to follow. The deal gives TrueLayer something its pay-by-bank rails have lacked: the ability to offer deferred payment alongside instant debit at checkout.

This is a strategically significant move for the account-to-account payments sector. Pay-by-bank networks have long struggled to match the consumer appeal of card-based checkout, where credit is built into the product. By combining open banking initiation with a credit layer, TrueLayer is attempting to close that gap directly rather than relying on merchants or third parties to bolt on financing.

The acquisition also reflects broader consolidation pressure. Open banking infrastructure providers that launched as pure-play data or payment initiation firms are finding that the economics of initiation alone are thin. Adding credit, which carries margin and deepens the merchant relationship, is a logical next step. Whether TrueLayer can underwrite effectively in a regulated credit market will be the harder question.

*Sources: [TrueLayer buys fintech In3, offering users debit and credit at checkout](https://www.finextra.com/pressarticle/109975/truelayer-buys-fintech-in3-offering-users-debit-and-credit-at-checkout) — Finextra | [TrueLayer adds split-payment capabilities with In3 acquisition](https://www.fintechfutures.com/m-a/truelayer-acquires-in3) — FinTech Futures*

stories.original:
**Visa pledges €500m European investment as sovereignty debate intensifies**

*Visa's commitment to build local data processing infrastructure in Europe is a direct response to growing political pressure to reduce dependence on US payment networks.*

Visa has announced plans to invest €500 million in Europe, including the construction of a new local data processing centre. The move is explicitly framed as a response to the payments sovereignty debate that has gathered pace across the continent, with policymakers from the ECB and national central banks increasingly vocal about reducing reliance on non-European schemes.

The timing is pointed. Just days after the Bank of Finland framed European payment autonomy as a geopolitical imperative, and with Wero and other domestic alternatives gaining political backing, Visa is positioning itself as a partner rather than a dependency risk. A local data processing centre addresses one of the most concrete sovereignty concerns: that European transaction data is routed through and stored on US infrastructure.

Whether this mollifies policymakers remains to be seen. The sovereignty push is not primarily about data localisation — it is about control over payment infrastructure and the economic rents that flow from it. Visa's investment buys goodwill, but it does not change the fundamental dynamic that transaction economics on European card payments flow to two US companies. For Wero and EPI backers, that structural argument persists regardless of where Visa puts its servers.

*Sources: [As European payments sovereignty debate rages, Visa makes its case for place on continent](https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/47831/as-european-payments-sovereignty-debate-rages-visa-makes-its-case-for-place-on-continent) — Finextra*

**BIS and GLEIF prototype uses LEIs to streamline cross-border open finance**

*A joint BIS-GLEIF prototype demonstrates that legal entity identifiers embedded in open banking APIs can materially reduce KYC friction for SMEs making cross-border payments and opening foreign accounts.*

The Bank for International Settlements and the Global Legal Entity Identifier Foundation have built a working prototype showing how LEIs can be integrated into open banking and open finance APIs. The proof of concept focuses on two use cases: cross-border payment initiation and remote business account opening, both for SMEs. The core proposition is that a verified LEI, carried within the API call, reduces the need for duplicative KYC and anti-money laundering checks at each counterparty.

This is a practical step in a problem that has resisted easy solutions. Cross-border SME payments remain disproportionately expensive and slow, largely because of compliance friction rather than technical limitations. If LEIs can serve as a portable, machine-readable trust anchor across jurisdictions, they could reduce the manual verification that inflates costs and processing times.

The prototype sits alongside the BIS's broader work on cross-border tokenisation, reported earlier this week. Together, they suggest the BIS is systematically testing the building blocks of a more interoperable cross-border payments architecture, with open finance APIs and standardised identifiers as complementary layers. Whether banks and fintechs adopt LEIs at sufficient scale to make this work commercially is the open question; LEI uptake among SMEs has historically been low, driven largely by regulatory mandates rather than voluntary adoption.

*Sources: [BIS and GLEIF team on LEIs in cross-border open finance prototype](https://www.finextra.com/pressarticle/109982/bis-and-gleif-team-on-leis-in-cross-border-open-finance-prototype) — Finextra*
